title: Marshall Field & Co. v. Clark
lead: Importers attack their customs assessments by challenging the tariff act’s enactment and two different provisions elsewhere in the statute.

actors.name: Marshall Field & Co.
actors.role: Importer contesting duties on woolens and silk embroidery.

actors.name: John M. Clark
actors.role: Chicago collector who assessed Field’s duties.

actors.name: Boyd, Sutton & Co.; Herrman, Sternbach & Co.
actors.role: Importers bringing companion challenges to other goods’ duties.

actors.name: President Benjamin Harrison
actors.role: Approved the authenticated 1890 act; the act assigned the President reciprocity determinations.

proceedings: The Board of General Appraisers sustained the collectors’ assessments.
The respective federal circuit courts affirmed.
The Supreme Court affirmed each judgment; Lamar and Fuller disagreed on delegation but concurred in the results.
limits: The claimed tobacco-rebate omission was not a Supreme Court factual finding. Sugar-bounty constitutionality and constitutionally mandated journal entries were reserved. Agreement in judgments did not make the delegation analysis unanimous.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The importers seek refunds by attacking the 1890 tariff law
sections.cue: Which duties and other statutory provisions entered the controversy?
paragraphs: Marshall Field & Co. paid duties on woolen goods and silk embroideries to Chicago customs collector John M. Clark under the Tariff Act of October 1, 1890. Companion cases involved Boyd, Sutton & Co.’s silk and cotton laces and Herrman, Sternbach & Co.’s colored cotton cloths. Those proceedings also involved the United States and, in Boyd’s case, the New York collector. The importers hoped defects in other portions of the Act would invalidate their own assessments.

The Act generally admitted specified sugar, molasses, coffee, tea, and hides duty free. Beginning January 1, 1892, its reciprocity provision directed the President to suspend that treatment for a producing country whose exactions on American products he found reciprocally unequal and unreasonable. Congress specified the substitute duties; the President could determine suspension’s duration. Another provision paid Treasury bounties for domestic sugar production.

The importers also alleged that a tobacco-rebate provision passed both Houses but disappeared from the enrolled Act. The authenticated text bore both presiding officers’ signatures, President Benjamin Harrison’s approval, and archival deposit with the Secretary of State. They proposed journals, committee materials, and other congressional documents to prove the discrepancy. The Court did not find the omission actually occurred.

sections.title: Three challenges survive to the Supreme Court after the assessments are sustained
sections.cue: What did authentication establish, and what could judges still examine?
paragraphs: The importers protested to the Board of General Appraisers, which sustained the collectors. Federal circuit courts affirmed, and the Supreme Court considered the cases together. Justice Harlan separately addressed enactment, reciprocity, and bounties.

On enactment, the Court agreed that signatures could not constitutionally enact something Congress never passed. Its question was evidentiary: which official record conclusively established passage? The Journal Clause did not require full reproduction of every bill and amendment and left discretion over record detail. Attestation by both Houses’ presiding officers, presidential approval, and public deposit established the enacted text against this proposed contradiction through journals and related papers.

Respect for coordinate branches and legal stability supported the rule. Working journals could contain errors and omissions; allowing collateral impeachment endangered settled laws. Supporting state cases and contrary decisions shaped by different state constitutions did not all present the same question. Gardner v. Collector had used a journal to supply a missing approval year, not contradict an authenticated statute’s existence or terms.

Authentication did not immunize substance from constitutional review, as the Court’s remaining analysis demonstrated. It also reserved consequences where the Constitution specifically required a matter to be entered in a journal. The holding did not make every legislative proceeding immune from judicial examination.

sections.title: Harlan treats reciprocity as conditional legislation
sections.cue: Who selected the governing policy and its consequences?
paragraphs: The importers argued that the President received legislative or treaty-making power. Harlan relied on Aurora, which sustained statutory operation contingent on a presidential proclamation of later circumstances. Revival and suspension could both execute legal consequences Congress had prescribed.

The majority also surveyed embargo, nonintercourse, discriminatory-tonnage, reciprocal-trade, and unsafe-import legislation. Executive officials had long determined conditions triggering or suspending legislated restrictions. Practice carried interpretive weight despite differences among examples; it did not turn each historical act into independently adjudicated precedent.

Congress here selected goods, chose reciprocity, identified foreign exactions, and fixed alternative duties. The President’s judgment of unequal and unreasonable treatment identified the specified condition. Once found, suspension was obligatory. Harlan located the decision that suspension should occur in Congress, while the President determined when its conditions existed.

Duration still required judgment, but the majority understood it as administering enacted policy rather than choosing law. That distinction also answered the treaty objection: the President implemented legislation instead of substituting an executive treaty. Saying merely that he found facts misses the contested evaluative language and duration discretion on which the competing opinions focused.

sections.title: Lamar and Fuller see policy discretion, yet still sustain the importers’ duties
sections.cue: How did severability produce the same judgments despite disagreement?
paragraphs: Justice Lamar, joined by Chief Justice Fuller, accepted genuinely contingent legislation like Aurora but read this statute differently. Deciding which foreign treatment was reciprocally unequal and unreasonable and how long suspension was just required policy about American commercial relations. Breadth of affected American products and duration discretion made the assignment legislative rather than mere identification of an ascertainable event.

Lamar also questioned historical practice: many examples lacked judicial approval and could not overcome a clear constitutional prohibition. He and Fuller nevertheless considered reciprocity separable from the importers’ own duties, so their objection did not warrant refunds.

The Court resolved the sugar-bounty challenge through a similar independent severability inquiry without deciding Congress’s disputed bounty power. The question was whether Congress evidently would not enact valid provisions without the challenged ones. Import duties and domestic payments operated separately; a common protective economic purpose did not prove mutual legal dependence. The importers therefore could not defeat their assessments by attacking the bounty appropriation, and the broader General Welfare Clause question remained open.

On February 29, 1892, the Supreme Court affirmed each assessment judgment. The importers received no refund on these theories. The assigned excerpt centers delegation and Lamar’s disagreement, while the full opinion supplies enrollment and bounty analysis explaining the complete disposition. Neither authentication nor agreement in the result validated every component of the Act unanimously.
